newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Africans, U.N. express alarm over Savimbi's stalling.
newsitem.headline: Africans, U.N. express alarm over Savimbi's stalling.

text.p: With the Angola peace process stalled, African leaders and Security Council members on Thursday expressed alarm and threatened sanctions against the former rebel UNITA movement led by Jonas Savimbi.

"The council must send a clear unambiguous message to UNITA: Time is up, the game is over," said Zimbabwe's Foreign Minister I.S.G. Mudenge. "Apparently scheming, selfishness, greed and self-aggrandizement have stymied the peace process."

A resolution expected to be adopted on Friday calls for the council to consider by Nov. 20 such measures as freezing UNITA bank accounts abroad or restricting leaders' travel. The council has already imposed an oil and arms embargo but has had trouble enforcing it.

In a run-up to the vote, 32 countries debated the Angolan peace process, including ministers from the Southern African Development Community (SADC) countries, which organised a peace summit earlier this month that Savimbi boycotted.

SADC nations would like sanctions to kick in automatically next month if UNITA, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola, does not comply with the accords it signed. But envoys said the United States, Portugal and Russia, the resolution's sponsors, would probably oppose that.

Nevertheless, Savimbi, once supported by the former white South African government as well as the United States, received little sympathy from any of the speakers regardless of their position on the resolution.

"It is time now for UNITA to act boldly to take the remaining steps toward compliance with the obligations it set for itself," said U.S. envoy Karl Inderfurth, who noted that Secretary of State Warren Christopher would visit Angola early mext week.

Said Botswana's foreign minister, Lt.-Gen. Mompati Merafhee: "It is a matter of profound regret that the implementation of the Lusaka Protocol has reached a stalemate and it is clear that the gains of the last few months are in grave danger."

UNITA has delayed integrating 26,000 fighters into a national army with its former government enemies, interfered with U.N. peacekeepers deployed in their area and relinquished only old arms for those guerrillas being demobilized.

Savimbi also has rejected the vice presidency reserved for him under the peace accord, in part because it would have meant moving to government-held Luanda, far away from his base. He is also concerned about the government's alleged use of mercenaries, including South Africans who once fought on his side of the civil war.
The United Nations has a 7,200-member peacekeeping operation mission in Angola, its largest remaining mission, which may end in February.

It is helping implement the agreement signed in Lusaka, Zambia, in November 1994, ending nearly two decades of civil war between the Angolan government and UNITA. The council's draft resolution calls for only a two-month renewal of the peacekeeping force to keep up pressure on both parties.
